- When sentiment is strongly positive (e.g., >0.8) and forecast is high, reduce forecast slightly to avoid overreaction.  
- When sentiment is strongly negative (e.g., < -0.3) and forecast is low, raise forecast modestly to avoid underreaction.  
- If recent price history shows a sharp spike followed by a drop, model tends to overshoot — dampen forecast in the immediate aftermath.  
- If forecast consistently exceeds true outcome by 2–3% over 30-day horizon, apply a 1–2% downward bias adjustment.  
- If sentiment is volatile or mixed (±0.3–0.7), model often overfits short-term noise — smooth forecasts with a 3–5 day moving average.  
- When sentiment is flat or near-zero, model tends to overestimate mean reversion — adjust downward by 0.5–1.5% for 10-day horizon.  
- If forecast is significantly higher than 30-day moving average of history, reduce by 1–2% to avoid “mean-reversion overcorrection.”  
- For horizon > 15 days, model often underestimates downward momentum — add 0.5–1.5% upward bias if sentiment is negative.
